title: Should Warehouse Modernization Wait Until an SAP S/4HANA Migration Is Complete?
summary: For organizations managing maintenance inventory, spare parts, industrial materials, and other business-critical assets, these inefficiencies extend far beyond simple productivity concerns. They can impact inventory confidence, operational readiness, maintenance planning, and overall business performance.

# Should Warehouse Modernization Wait Until an SAP S/4HANA Migration Is Complete?

[About the author](https://www.linkedin.com/in/demianpeterson/)

Key Takeaways


- Warehouse modernization does not need to wait for SAP S/4HANA. Organizations can improve warehouse execution today by implementing an SAP-native execution layer while broader Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) transformation programs continue.
- Warehouse transformation initiatives are most successful when organizations focus on optimizing workflows first and then apply enabling mobile technologies.
- Modern execution platforms and enterprise mobility solutions can improve inventory accuracy, user adoption, and productivity without disrupting long-term SAP modernization strategies.


## The Warehouse Doesn't Stop Operating During ERP Transformation


Many organizations are balancing two critical priorities at the same time: modernizing warehouse operations while preparing for or executing a multi-year SAP S/4HANA transformation.


Because ERP modernization programs often consume significant IT resources, operational improvement initiatives are frequently delayed. Warehouse modernization is one of the most common areas placed on hold.


The assumption is understandable. If a major ERP transformation is underway, many leaders believe it makes sense to wait until the migration is complete before addressing warehouse execution challenges.


In reality, warehouse operations continue every day regardless of where an organization sits in its SAP roadmap.


Materials are received, stored, moved, counted, picked, shipped, and consumed. Technicians, production teams, field personnel, and supply chain stakeholders all depend on accurate inventory data and efficient execution. Business challenges do not pause simply because a larger ERP initiative is underway.


As a result, postponing warehouse improvements often means extending inefficiencies, training challenges, inventory inaccuracies, and productivity losses for months or even years longer than necessary.


## Why Some Organizations Are Freezing the Wrong Projects


Many legacy SAP mobile environments were originally designed around transactions rather than worker workflows.


Employees are often required to select the correct transaction, navigate multiple screens, manually enter information the system already knows, and make decisions that software could automate or guide.


For organizations managing maintenance inventory, spare parts, industrial materials, and other business-critical assets, these inefficiencies extend far beyond simple productivity concerns. They can impact inventory confidence, operational readiness, maintenance planning, and overall business performance.


Warehouse personnel frequently spend more time interacting with systems than performing value-added work.


Training requirements increase because employees must learn application behavior instead of focusing on operational processes. New hires take longer to become productive, while experienced employees often rely on tribal knowledge and workarounds to compensate for process complexity.


Waiting for a future ERP milestone does little to address these operational challenges.


## A Warehouse Execution Layer Doesn't Need to Wait for S/4HANA


One of the most important concepts operations and supply chain leaders should understand is this:


It is possible to modernize warehouse execution immediately by implementing an SAP-native execution layer.


Rather than replacing SAP, this approach enhances the execution experience while allowing SAP to remain the system of record.


A warehouse execution layer simplifies complex processes, incorporates business rules directly into workflows, and guides workers through tasks using intuitive mobile experiences. Instead of requiring employees to know which transaction should come next, the software presents the appropriate steps within the context of the work being performed.


This type of approach can operate across SAP ERP Central Component (ECC) environments, transitional hybrid landscapes, and SAP S/4HANA deployments.


For example, solutions such as Havensight's Inventory One are designed to support organizations throughout different stages of their SAP modernization journey while maintaining alignment with future ERP initiatives.


The key takeaway is that warehouse execution improvements and ERP transformation programs do not need to compete for value. In many cases, they can progress together.


## A Better Approach: Workflow First, Technology Second


Many warehouse modernization initiatives begin with technology selection.


A better approach begins by identifying the operational challenge.


Instead of asking:


*"Which device should we buy?"*


Organizations should ask:


*"Which business problem are we trying to solve?"*


This shift ensures technology investments support measurable operational outcomes.


### 1. Identify the Operational Challenge


Many warehouse environments experience common operational issues, including:


- Excessive manual data entry
- Receiving and picking errors
- Inconsistent inventory execution
- Limited real-time visibility
- Lengthy training cycles
- Variability across locations and shifts


Modernization discussions should begin with these challenges rather than hardware specifications.


### 2. Optimize the Workflow


Once operational challenges are identified, workflows can be redesigned to incorporate automation, business validations, process guidance, and mobile execution.


Well-designed workflows reduce unnecessary decision-making, simplify execution, and improve consistency regardless of worker experience or location.


The objective is to create processes that guide users naturally rather than requiring them to memorize transactions, procedures, and exceptions.


### 3. Enable the Right Mobile Technologies


After workflows have been optimized, mobile technologies become valuable extensions of the process.


Examples include:


**Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Intelligent Data Capture**
Capture information from documents, labels, and packing slips and convert it directly into operational data.


**Dimensioning**
Automatically measure packages and materials during normal receiving and storage activities.


**Image Capture**
Document damage, condition, compliance requirements, and transaction verification as part of everyday operations.


**Advanced Barcode Scanning**
Improve speed, accuracy, and traceability across receiving, inventory management, picking, transfers, and shipping.


**Wearable Mobile Computing**
Support high-volume environments where hands-free operation and worker productivity are critical.


These technologies become significantly more valuable when embedded into optimized workflows rather than deployed as standalone capabilities.


For example, enterprise-grade mobile devices from providers such as Zebra Technologies can capture dimensions, images, and inventory data during normal warehouse activities without introducing additional process steps.


### 4. Select the Appropriate Form Factor


Only after workflows and business requirements are defined should organizations determine which device best fits the operation.


Depending on the process, the right answer may be a handheld computer, wearable device, rugged tablet, or vehicle-mounted solution.


The workflow should determine the technology strategy, not the other way around.


## Why Mobile Dimensioning Is Receiving More Attention


One capability attracting growing interest across asset-intensive industries is mobile dimensioning.


Many organizations maintain inventory records with incomplete, estimated, or outdated dimensional data. As a result, activities such as storage planning, inventory placement, warehouse utilization, and replenishment planning become more difficult than necessary.


Modern imaging and dimensioning technologies allow workers to capture dimensional information during normal warehouse activities rather than through separate measurement processes.


The outcome can include:


- More accurate master data
- Improved warehouse space utilization
- Better inventory placement decisions
- Increased planning accuracy
- Reduced manual effort


For many organizations, dimensioning delivers benefits that extend well beyond warehouse efficiency. Accurate physical inventory characteristics help support stronger supply chain planning and more effective inventory management across the enterprise.


## A Different Perspective for Organizations Newer to SAP


Not every organization has decades of SAP warehouse history.


Many organizations have adopted SAP more recently and therefore approach warehouse modernization with a different set of expectations.


Long-tenured SAP users often carry assumptions shaped by legacy mobile applications and transaction-heavy processes. Even when those tools are inefficient, they are familiar.


Organizations newer to SAP often expect a different experience. Their expectation is a modern, guided, mobile-first environment that simplifies execution and accelerates adoption from the outset.


This perspective is helping drive broader interest in execution-layer technology and workflow-based modernization strategies.


## What IT Leaders Should Consider


Operations teams naturally focus on productivity, inventory accuracy, user adoption, and process consistency.


IT leaders tend to focus on a different set of questions:


- How difficult will the solution be to support?
- Will it align with long-term SAP strategy?
- Does it increase integration complexity?
- Will it create future technical debt?


Solutions that maintain SAP as the system of record while operating within the SAP landscape can help address many of these concerns.


From an architectural perspective, organizations are increasingly prioritizing approaches that:


- Simplify governance
- Reduce integration complexity
- Eliminate unnecessary points of failure
- Accelerate deployment timelines
- Support future ERP roadmaps
- Lower long-term ownership costs


These considerations become especially important when IT teams are already dedicating substantial resources to broader SAP transformation initiatives.


## Modernization Should Follow Business Needs, Not ERP Timelines


Organizations no longer need to choose between operational improvement and ERP transformation.


Modern warehouse execution platforms allow teams to improve inventory accuracy, streamline workflows, increase user adoption, and enhance operational consistency while remaining aligned with long-term SAP strategies.


When combined with technologies such as OCR, advanced barcode scanning, dimensioning, image capture, and wearable computing, organizations can modernize warehouse operations without waiting for every phase of a broader ERP program to be completed.


Solutions such as Havensight's Inventory One and Zebra Technologies demonstrate how organizations are modernizing execution environments while preserving SAP as the system of record.


The broader lesson is simple: **warehouse modernization should be driven by operational needs, not postponed because of future ERP milestones.**


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Can organizations modernize warehouse operations before migrating to SAP S/4HANA?**


Yes. Organizations can improve warehouse execution, inventory accuracy, and workforce productivity before completing an SAP S/4HANA migration by implementing solutions that support both current and future SAP environments.


**What is a warehouse execution layer?**


A warehouse execution layer sits between warehouse workers and SAP transactions, guiding users through optimized workflows while SAP remains the system of record. The result is simplified execution, fewer errors, faster adoption, and more consistent operational performance.


**Why should organizations focus on workflows before selecting hardware?**


Technology delivers the most value when it supports a well-defined process. Identifying operational challenges first helps ensure that devices, software, and automation investments directly address business objectives.


**How can mobile technologies improve warehouse operations?**


Modern mobile technologies support capabilities such as barcode scanning, OCR, image capture, dimensioning, wearable computing, and real-time data collection. When integrated into operational workflows, these tools can improve efficiency, accuracy, and visibility.


**Does warehouse modernization create risk for an SAP S/4HANA migration?**


Not necessarily. Solutions that maintain SAP as the system of record and align with SAP architecture strategies can support operational improvements while remaining compatible with broader ERP transformation programs.


## Should you wait for SAP S/4HANA to modernize your warehouse?


Warehouse modernization does not need to wait for SAP S/4HANA. Organizations can improve inventory accuracy, workforce productivity, and warehouse execution today by implementing an SAP-native execution layer while broader ERP transformation initiatives continue. By focusing on workflow optimization first and then applying mobile technologies such as OCR, scanning, image capture, dimensioning, and wearable computing, organizations can modernize operations without disrupting long-term SAP strategies. Solutions such as Havensight's Inventory One and Zebra Technologies serve as examples of how enterprises are improving warehouse execution while preserving SAP as the system of record.
